---
title: "Oxygen Functions"
description: "Server-side TypeScript handlers that ship inside your Oxygen app and run on Oxygen's managed runtime"
---

**Oxygen Functions** are TypeScript handlers that ship *inside* your
[SDK app](/guide/build/sdk) and run **server-side** on Oxygen's managed V8
isolate runtime, with direct access to your project's data plane. Reach for them
whenever the browser shouldn't do the work itself:

- a parameterized or privileged warehouse query,
- a **warehouse write** (insert / upsert / exec),
- kicking off an [Airway ELT](/guide/build/data-infrastructure) run,
- an outbound API call to a third-party service.

No separate backend to stand up — a function is versioned and deployed with your
frontend by `oxyc publish`.

<Note>
An Oxygen Function is a bundled TypeScript handler — **not** a YAML
[Automation](/guide/build/automations) task or a Data App `task`. It runs with
the app's project-level access, not the invoking visitor's — with one exception,
[`ctx.warehouse` writes to a managed warehouse](#who-a-write-runs-as).
</Note>

## Authoring a function

A function is a file at `functions/<name>.ts` that exports a default
`async (req, ctx) => Response`, declared in the app's `oxy-app.json`:

<Note>
  The **status** you return is the status the caller sees. `useFunction`'s
  `invoke` resolves on a 2xx and **rejects** on anything else, with a
  `FunctionError` carrying `status`, the parsed `body`, and any logs the run
  captured — so `return Response.json({ error: "…" }, { status: 409 })` is a
  rejection the caller can branch on, not a value it has to inspect.

  ```ts
  try {
    await invoke({ pathId });
  } catch (e) {
    const err = e as FunctionError;
    if (err.status === 409) { /* already assigned */ }
  }
  ```

  Requires `@oxy-hq/sdk` 2.10 or later. Before that the status was discarded and
  every response resolved.
</Note>

```ts functions/daily-rollup.ts
export default async function (req, ctx) {
  const { rows } = await ctx.query(
    "SELECT date, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY 1"
  );
  await ctx.warehouse.upsert("daily_revenue", rows);
  ctx.log(`rolled up ${rows.length} days`);
  return Response.json({ ok: true, days: rows.length });
}
```

```json oxy-app.json
{
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "slug": "store-pulse",
  "functions": {
    "daily-rollup": { "route": true, "timeoutSeconds": 30 },
    "stripe-sync":  { "schedule": "0 * * * *", "timezone": "UTC" }
  }
}
```

- **`req`** is `{ method, headers, body }` — `body` is the raw request body as
  a string, and header names are lower-case. A scheduled or Airway run sees
  `POST` with no headers. `Response` / `Response.json(...)` are polyfilled by
  the runtime.
- **`ctx`** is the data plane:
  - `ctx.query` / `ctx.queryStream` — read-only, row-capped SQL. `ctx.query`
    resolves to `{ rows, truncated }`
  - `ctx.semantic.query` — a [semantic-model](/guide/build/semantic-model/simple-model) query
  - `ctx.warehouse.query(db, sql)` and `ctx.warehouse.{insert, exec, upsert}` — reads, and writes allowlisted by `destinations`
  - `ctx.airhouse` — append the app's own facts (see [Where data goes](#where-data-goes))
  - `ctx.oltp` — read and write the app's own records
  - `ctx.storage` — the app's file storage
  - `ctx.airway.run` — kick off an ELT pipeline
  - `ctx.fetch` — outbound HTTP, SSRF-allowlisted, HTTPS-only, size/time-capped
  - `ctx.env` — per-app secrets; `ctx.secrets.set` writes them back
  - `ctx.email.send` — email the app's users
  - `ctx.org.people()` — the org's people directory, read-only
  - `ctx.crypto.{hmac, verifyHmac, timingSafeEqual}` — synchronous HMAC helpers (SHA-256 and hex by default)
  - `ctx.user`, `ctx.log`

Capabilities that reach beyond the app's own reads are **off until the
function's manifest entry declares them** — see [Capabilities](#capabilities).

## Where data goes

Pick the store by the shape of the data:

| The data | Store | In a function | Declare |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Facts** — something happened and won't change: an order, a completed checklist | The workspace's Airhouse, in the schema `app_<slug>` | `ctx.airhouse.append(table, rows)`, `ctx.airhouse.query(sql)`, `ctx.airhouse.exec(sql)` | function: `"airhouse": { "enabled": true }`; app: `"airhouseMigrations": { "dir": "airhouse-migrations" }` |
| **Records** the app edits — bookings, assignments, templates | The org's OLTP Postgres, in the schema `app_<slug>` | `ctx.oltp.query(sql, params)`, `ctx.oltp.exec(sql, params)`, `ctx.oltp.tx(async (tx) => …)` | function: `"oltp": { "enabled": true }`; app: `"migrations": { "dir": "migrations" }` |
| **Files** — photos, PDFs, exports | The app's storage | `ctx.storage` | function: `"storage": { "read": true, "write": true }` |
| **The customer's warehouse** — ClickHouse, Snowflake, BigQuery, their Postgres | Theirs | `ctx.query`, `ctx.warehouse.query(db, sql)` | read-only (see below) |

`<slug>` is the app's slug with `-` replaced by `_` (`store-ops` →
`app_store_ops`). The schema is always derived from the slug — a manifest can't
name another app's schema. Tables are created by the SQL files in the declared
migrations directory when the app is published. `ctx.airhouse` and `ctx.oltp`
write **as the app**, whoever invoked the function, so a scheduled run writes
the same way a click does.

Airhouse tables take no primary keys, unique constraints, or indexes, so give
every fact the id its source assigned plus a `recorded_at`, and record
corrections as new facts rather than updates. For records, always use bound
parameters (`$1`, `$2`), and put statements that must land together in one
`ctx.oltp.tx`.

```ts functions/complete-checklist.ts
export default async function (req, ctx) {
  const { runId, storeGuid } = JSON.parse(req.body);
  await ctx.oltp.tx(async (tx) => {
    await tx.exec("UPDATE checklist_runs SET status = 'done' WHERE id = $1", [runId]);
    await tx.exec("DELETE FROM open_reminders WHERE run_id = $1", [runId]);
  });
  await ctx.airhouse.append("checklist_completions", [
    { completion_id: runId, store_guid: storeGuid, completed_by: ctx.user.id, recorded_at: new Date().toISOString() },
  ]);
  return Response.json({ ok: true });
}
```

## Who a write runs as

Reads always run with the app's project-level access, and `ctx.airhouse` /
`ctx.oltp` always write as the app. `ctx.warehouse` writes to an
**Oxygen-managed warehouse** are the one place the *invoker* matters: the
connection is opened with a short-lived credential whose role follows the
workspace role of the person who called the function.

| Invoker | May write a managed warehouse? |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace **Owner** or **Admin** | yes |
| Workspace **Member** or **Viewer** | no — the same answer they'd get querying it directly |
| A **scheduled**, **Airway-step**, or **webhook** run (no human caller) | no — use `ctx.airhouse` instead |

A denied write surfaces as a permission error on the statement (`Reader role
cannot execute Update statements`) while queries in the same function keep
working — that combination means the *caller's* role, not a broken
`destinations` allowlist.

### Customer warehouses are read-only

Databases you configure with your own credentials (BigQuery, Snowflake,
ClickHouse, …) are **read-only** to functions. A write to one is refused unless
the function lists the database in `destinations` **and** says why in
`customerWarehouseWrites`:

```json oxy-app.json
"functions": {
  "post-journal": {
    "destinations": ["clickhouse"],
    "customerWarehouseWrites": {
      "clickhouse": "Journal entries stay beside the legacy ClickHouse facts until they move to Airhouse"
    }
  }
}
```

Prefer moving the data instead: facts to `ctx.airhouse`, records to `ctx.oltp`.

## Capabilities

Each function's entry in `oxy-app.json` declares what it may do. Every
capability is **fail-closed** — omit it and the call is rejected before any
connection is opened.

| Manifest key | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| `destinations: ["<db>", …]` | `ctx.warehouse` writes to those databases |
| `customerWarehouseWrites: { "<db>": "<reason>" }` | Writes to a customer warehouse (also list it in `destinations`) |
| `airhouse: { enabled: true }` | `ctx.airhouse` |
| `oltp: { enabled: true }` | `ctx.oltp` (the org's OLTP store must be provisioned first) |
| `storage: { read, write }` | `ctx.storage` reads and writes |
| `secrets: { write: true }` | `ctx.secrets.set`, limited to the app's own secrets |
| `email: { send: true }` | `ctx.email.send`. The sender is platform-controlled; a function may set `replyTo` but not `from` |
| `org: { read: true }` | `ctx.org.people()` — names and roles, no contact details |

Other per-function keys: `route`, `schedule` and `timezone`, `airwayStep`,
`webhook` (see [Webhooks](#webhooks)), `timeoutSeconds`, `cache`, and
`retries` — `{ maxAttempts, minTimeoutMs, maxTimeoutMs }` for scheduled and
background runs (route calls are never retried).

`oxyc publish` refuses a function that calls a `ctx` capability its manifest
entry doesn't declare.

## Invocation modes

A function can be reached three ways, each with its own identity and default
timeout (a ceiling; max 300s):

| Mode | Declared as | Identity | Default timeout |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Route** | `"route": true` | the visitor | 10s |
| **Schedule** | `"schedule": "<cron>"` | system | 60s |
| **Airway step** | used as an Airway transform | system | 300s |

The route endpoint (`POST /customer-apps/<org>/<slug>/fn/<name>`) is **POST-only**
(405 otherwise), rate-limited per `(user, app, function)`, and every invocation
is audited.

## Webhooks

A function can receive an unauthenticated POST from a third party — a payment
provider, a delivery platform — by declaring a `webhook` block:

```json oxy-app.json
"functions": {
  "orders-webhook": {
    "route": false,
    "webhook": {
      "secretVar": "UBER_WEBHOOK_SECRET",
      "signatureHeader": "x-uber-signature",
      "encoding": "hex"
    }
  }
}
```

The sender posts to `POST /api/webhooks/apps/<org>/<app>/<name>`. **Oxygen
verifies every request** — an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body, keyed by the app
secret named in `secretVar`, compared in constant time against
`signatureHeader` — before the function is queued, so your code never sees an
unverified request. `secretVar` may hold several comma-separated keys, so a
provider's key rotation doesn't drop events. A verified request is answered
`202` immediately and the function runs in the background with no invoking
user. Without a `webhook` block the endpoint answers `404`.

## Calling a route function from React

Use the `useFunction` hook to invoke a `route` function imperatively — e.g. from
a button:

```tsx
import { useFunction } from "@oxy-hq/sdk";

function RefreshButton() {
  const rollup = useFunction("daily-rollup");
  return (
    <button disabled={rollup.isLoading} onClick={() => rollup.invoke({ full: true })}>
      {rollup.isLoading ? "Refreshing…" : "Refresh"}
    </button>
  );
}
```

- `invoke(body?, { idempotencyKey? })` returns the function's JSON response.
- `rollup.data` holds the last successful result; `rollup.error` the last error.
- Concurrent identical invokes are **deduplicated** into one request.

## Caching

Results are **not cached by default** — functions are often side-effectful. A
read-only function can opt into a server result cache by adding
`"cache": { "ttlSeconds": N }` to its manifest entry; the cache is keyed per
`(build, user, body)`, invalidated by the next publish, and bypassed with
`?refresh`.
